newsitem.title: USA: Fed weighs costs/benefits in looking ahead - G'span.
newsitem.headline: Fed weighs costs/benefits in looking ahead - G'span.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan said the Fed had to weigh carefully the costs and benefits of any pre-emptive shifts in monetary policy.

"What we try to do...is to try to make judgements about the relative probabalities of what the outlook is and then sort of array a series of different types of monetary policy moves and make judgements -- not only what they would contribute if that forecast is correct but also what is the cost if we are wrong," he told Congress's Joint Economic Committee.
"And clearly, if we find that if the costs of being wrong are substantial, relative to the potential benefits, that would argue for not moving in a certain direction," he added.
Nevertheless, Greenspan said the Fed had to forecast where the economy was headed and act on that forecast.
"We have no choice but to forecast and act upon a forecast," he said, "..unless we do that, we will be behind the curve a good deal of the time.
"Monetary policy in years past has been demonstrably counter productive in certain periods, largely because we were too late in moving," he said.
Greenspan, in answer to a separate question, said there was no compelling evidence that the nation's trade deficit affected interest rates.
Although he did say that a strong dollar, other things being equal, worked to increase the trade deficit.
"It is certainly the case that the stronger the dollar, other things equal, I emphasize other things equal, the greater the trade deficit," he said.
"There is no evidence that I find compelling which, however, suggests that the trade deficit itself has a material effect one way or the other on interest rates," he said.
